germane

jer-MAYN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Germane is directly relevant to the subject or matter being discussed.

The editor cut an entire paragraph from the article because it simply wasn't germane to the story's main argument.

Example

During the job interview, the hiring manager only asked questions germane to the actual responsibilities of the position, never anything personal.

Germane isn't just about being interesting or true -- it's specifically about being closely connected to the exact topic at hand.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

relevant: Relevant means having a real bearing on the matter at hand -- a relevant fact deserves at least a mention. Germane is stricter: directly on the exact subject under discussion, close enough to belong in the conversation. Plenty of relevant background never becomes germane to the point being decided.

pertinent: Pertinent describes information with a clear, practical bearing on the question being settled -- pertinent facts push a decision forward. Germane stresses fit with the topic itself: a germane remark belongs to the subject, whether or not it settles anything. Pertinent points toward an answer; germane stays on the subject.

applicable: Applicable describes a rule, law, or method that can be applied to a particular case -- it works there. Germane describes a remark or detail that belongs to the subject being discussed. A safety code can be applicable to a building without being germane to tonight's debate about parking.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

off-topic: straying from the subject being discussed

unrelated: having no real connection to something

Where it sits · how strongly it connects to the topic

related → germane → essential

related vs. germane: Something related to a topic has some connection to it, but the link may be loose -- weaker than being fully germane.

essential vs. germane: Something essential to a topic is absolutely necessary to understanding it, a stronger claim than merely being germane.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together: Germane comes from Latin germanus, meaning 'of the same parents' or 'closely related' -- it does not share a root with the word germ (seed), despite looking similar. Something germane to a topic is as closely, relevantly connected to it as a full sibling is to their own brother or sister.

Use the root in a new word: cousin-german: In old legal documents, your first cousin was sometimes called your 'cousin-german' to distinguish a full cousin from a more distant relation.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Watch out: germane looks like it should be related to germ (a seed or a microbe), but the two words come from completely different Latin roots -- it's a false friend, not a family connection.
